I'm a Linux noob trying to learn the command line. So I'm always looking out for things to try my new skills on.

Most people learn the command line at codeacademy.org I learned on overthewire.org It has more hacker-like scratch your own itch type of approach, highly recommended.

I also have a pet peeve, a web site that tries to prevent me from saving a picture. These piss me off to no end. So I came across this site which has nice old technical plans from the Victorian era. Good for a wallpaper or a printout.

The problem is that they have gone to great lengths trying to prevent people from saving the pictures. All pictures are chopped up in small chunks to make the whole thing inconvenient.

On windows I would have probably tried to download all the chunks using DownThemAll or something similar and then try to stitch them back together using Photoshop. So much work for so little reward, not my style.

This is Linux so lets try to use the command line and do the things the clever way.

Firs a bit of reconnaissance... Hmmm Seems like the chunks are 257px squares named X_Y.jpg starting from 0_0.jpg and ending with 20_11.jpg

252 images total. So lets download them all.

wget http://www.networkrail.co.uk/Digital_Archive/SeaDragon_images/NRCA110018S/GeneratedImages/dzc_output_files/13/{0..20}_{0..11}.jpg
 
[.....]
 
FINISHED
Total wall clock time: 37s
Downloaded: 252 files, 6.5M in 17s (381 KB/s)

Single command 252 files downloaded. Not bad for a noob.

Note to self: Next time try not to do it in your home folder you dumbass.

BTW. {0..20} means range from 0 to 20. Very neat.

Now lets stitch them all together...on the command line! The tool for this job seems to be ImageMagic so lets install that first. Image magic has no GUI, it works on the command line, so if you want your web script to convert images into thumbnails or avatars you use ImageMagic. (I'm just Googling stuff and writing what I see)

ImageMagic has a tool called convert which can stitch images like convert a.jpg b.jpg c.jpg -append abc.jpg where -append means columns and +append means rows. We need to do one of each in order to get the whole picture. Again, just Googling stuff.

Since I have so many images it would be nice to put the convert stuff in a loop. Bash can do loops as I learned a while ago, so lets try some. Because we start counting with 0 we have 21 columns and 12 rows.

for row in {0..11}
>do
> convert {0..20}_$row.jpg +append row$row.jpg
>done

Bingo! row0.jpg to row11.jpg stitched together! Damn I feel like I just leveled up!

Now to stitch the rows into columns. Note we are using -append now.

convert row{0..11}.jpg -append final_result.jpg

Aaaand here is the final_result.jpg

./feelsgoodman.sh

This is the abstract:

Obesity-linked insulin resistance greatly increases the risk for type 2 diabetes, hypertension, dyslipidemia, and nonalcoholic fatty liver disease, together known as the metabolic or insulin resistance syndrome. How obesity promotes insulin resistance remains incompletely understood. Plasma concentrations of free fatty acids and proinflammatory cytokines, endoplasmic reticulum ( ER) stress, and oxidative stress are all elevated in obesity and have been shown to induce insulin resistance. However, they may be late events that only develop after chronic excessive nutrient intake. The nature of the initial event that produces insulin resistance at the beginning of excess caloric intake and weight gain remains unknown. We show that feeding healthy men with ~6000 kcal/day of the common U.S. diet [~50% carbohydrate (CHO), ~ 35% fat, and ~15% protein] for 1 week produced a rapid weight gain of 3.5 kg and the rapid onset (after 2 to 3 days) of systemic and adipose tissue insulin resistance and oxidative stress but no inflammatory or ER stress. In adipose tissue, the oxidative stress resulted in extensive oxidation and carbonylation of numerous proteins, including carbonylation of GLUT4 near the glucose transport channel, which likely resulted in loss of GLUT4 activity. These results suggest that the initial event caused by overnutrition may be oxidative stress, which produces insulin resistance, at least in part, via carbonylation and oxidation-induced inactivation of GLUT4.
